title: Datacenter Systems Spending To Go Through The Roof In 2027
author: Timothy Prickett Morgan
text:
COMPUTE

Datacenter Systems Spending To Go Through The Roof In 2027

Timothy Prickett Morgan

Timothy Prickett
Morgan

Co-Editor, Co-Founder, The Next Platform

Published
tue 10 Nov 2026 // 00:28 UTC

It was a rough couple of days for the datacenter business in the wake of the elections in the United States last week, but the optimism about the future will very likely continue unabated. Right up to the moment when it might not.Just ahead of the election, the analysts and market researchers revised their IT spending forecast for 2026, which is damned near done now, and provided its first forecast for 2027, which looks like a killer year for IT spending. There are more than a few prognosticators who think that next year will be the peak and not because demand is not expected to be crazy after that but rather because there is a political uprising against tech titans and their datacenter and electricity needs at the same time that it was looking increasingly unlikely that electricity generation and distribution could be ramped up enough to meet datacenter demand in 2030, but less in 2028.

NEXTPLATFORM AD

There is a lot that can and cannot happen in 2028, and it remains difficult to predict the future much further out than twelve to eighteen months out given the wonkiness and wobbliness of the data right now and in the near term, which drives the forecast further out.That said, people make plans for their own IT spending based against the forecasts that IDC, Gartner, and others make, so it is important to be aware of how these forecasts change over time and how growth breaks down across the different segments of the IT economy.Without further ado, here is the Gartner IT spending forecast for 2026 and 2027:

One new twist has been added with the November 2026 forecast, and it is a useful one. Gartner has extracted Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS) cloudy compute, storage, and networking rentals out of the vast IT services segment as its own category. Now, we can see the revenues from the sale of datacenter systems (again: servers, storage, and networking hardware and their embedded operating systems software) as well as rental of such capacity.

NEXTPLATFORM AD

Gartner only gave figures for 2026 and 2027 for this new category, but we can use the percent change to work out IaaS spending in 2025 and extract it out of the IT services spending. Moreover, if you scan the Internet, you can find Gartner IaaS spending figures from 2015 through 2024. I have added those to my monster table and made estimates of where IaaS spending was globally in 2012, 2013, and 2014 to complete the dataset. All of these figures were then extracted from the overall IT services figures we have compiled over more than a decade from Gartner so we can see the longer trend of spending for IaaS rentals and IT services without IaaS.Take a gander:

Now that is a table. . . .Here is the neat thing that immediately leaps out of this table to me: For the longest time, enterprise software revenues were 2X to 3X the size of datacenter systems sales. But the advent of truly ridiculously expensive AI systems and the huge amount of spending on them as well as the upgrades to back office (transactional) and front office (data analytics and customer engagement) systems that feed into the AI systems has the combined spending on datacenter systems plus IaaS surpassing enterprise software next year – $1.73 trillion for the hardware spending, up 48 percent year on year, compared to $1.68 trillion for enterprise software, up a very normal 14.7 percent.

NEXTPLATFORM AD

The other neat bit is that spending on IT services minus IaaS will be in the same ballpark next year in Gartner’s forecast, up a more anemic 4.9 percent but still almost 2X as fast as global gross domestic product growth. It has been my contention after decades of watching IT spending trends that mature markets tend to grow at around 2X that of GDP.For those of you who like to think visually, here is the trends for the segments of spending that together make up what I call core IT:

That’s systems, enterprise software, and services. For all the talk of Appmageddon or Softwaremageddon or what have you, as you can see enterprise software spending has been on a new binge level even before the coronavirus pandemic hit in March 2020, and it looks like it really got going for a new and steeper line starting around 2017. The enterprise software line is not steepening, like spending for datacenter systems has been doing. But as you can also plainly see, Gartner thinks that the growth rate for spending on datacenter systems is going to cool in 2027 to a mere 55.4 percent after an explosive 2026 where growth was 73.8 percent. The average growth rate for datacenter systems revenues between 2013 and 2021 inclusive was a mere 2.3 percent, which compared unfavorably to an average global GDP of 2.7 percent over the same time. The systems market was beyond mature until the pandemic hit and then GenAI exploded on the scene as we came out of it in 2022.Core IT spending was not driven by servers, storage, and networking throughout most of this dataset – it was enterprise software and IT services that were in the driver’s seat and riding shotgun. Datacenter systems was in the trunk with duct tape over its mouth and zip ties on its hands and feet. (There’s an image for you. . . . ) The big change is that companies are becoming less stingy with the hardware budget because they can’t afford to miss the GenAI wave. In this regard, the GenAI boom most definitely resembles the Dot Com boom. But this time around, the hyperscalers and cloud builders already exist and they are hogging the allocations for GPUs and XPUs.

NEXTPLATFORM AD

The world has changed so much in this decade and a half. Back in 2012, Core IT spending was a little more than a third of overall IT spending, and as 2027 comes to a close, Core IT will account for more than two thirds of the total. The resulting gap between global GDP growth and Core IT spending growth is not 2X, which is normal-ish, but more like 8X in 2026 and 7.3X in 2027, if the spending and the GDP figures pan out as Gartner and the World Bank expect, respectively.We are not living in normal times, clearly.Now, with a dataset that spans so many years, it is interesting to ponder how much of the increase in IT budget change is due to inflation and how much is due to capacity expansion. To get a feel for that, I have inflation adjusted the datacenter spending figures using the 2021 dollar as the fulcrum.

Now, this chart is just expressing currency inflation, not price inflation due to too much demand chasing too little supply. It is hard to say for sure, but it seems like about half the growth in datacenter systems spending this year is due to supply-demand issues, which drives up prices, and half is due to the increase in supply that chip and system makers can actually deliver to meet some of that demand. But that is just an educated guess.This is just as bad as trying to buy plywood and two by fours or contractor services during the coronavirus pandemic. I know, because Nicole and I had to do major house repairs at that time and that was a very unfortunate time for that, let me assure you.
